analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health insurance plan covering every American, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and most private coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with just two cosponsors in April 1992, it received one hearing in the Senate Finance Committee in June and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have entitle every U.S. resident to a full package of health care and long-term care — hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, mental health, nursing home care — at little or no out-of-pocket cost. It would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, and CHAMPUS, and barred employers from deducting the cost of any health plan other than the public one, effectively shutting private insurers out of the main market. It would have been paid for by progressive premiums on individuals and by employer premiums scaled to each employer's size and profitability, funneled through State programs overseen by a new Federal Health Board.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident would gain guaranteed coverage with no dollar limits, no pre-existing condition screening, and free choice of provider, including long-term care that today can exhaust a family's savings. Providers would be paid by a single public payer, and the bill required payment to constitute payment in full, ending balance billing of patients.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every resident citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to covered health care and long-term care services, with automatic enrollment at birth or at establishment of residence [S2][S3].

Covers inpatient and outpatient hospital care, professional services, preventive care, prescription drugs, substance abuse and outpatient mental health services, hospice, rehabilitation, and even board-approved experimental treatment, and bars states from limiting the amount, duration, or scope of covered services [S2][S3].
Requires states to protect the income and assets of people using long-term care, so that a person can keep their home and their spouse is not impoverished by a nursing home stay [S2][S3].
Provides that payment by the state program is payment in full — no individual can be billed for any covered service except board-set copayments — and guarantees freedom to choose practitioners [S3].

Prohibits states from restricting timely access to medically necessary services or allowing queues with life-threatening potential, and bars residence waiting periods longer than three months [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals would pay a progressive, income-based premium and employers would pay premiums scaled to workforce size and profitability, collected by a new Federal Health Board. Employers would lose the tax deduction for group health plans unless those plans are the public program, ending the current tax-favored employer insurance system. Private insurers could sell only supplemental coverage, not coverage of services the plan already covers.

drawbacks.text: Every individual and employer would pay new American Health Security Plan premiums, with employer contributions sized to keep total household health spending from rising above its 1992 share — a real tax on employers and higher earners even as out-of-pocket costs fall [S2][S3].

The transition would terminate Medicare and Medicaid and eliminate the tax-favored employer health plan, so tens of millions of people with existing coverage would be moved onto an untested new system administered by newly created state agencies [S2][S3].

Hospitals and doctors would be paid through negotiated global budgets and fee schedules rather than market billing, which controls costs but gives providers less say over their revenue — a trade-off an honest supporter must acknowledge [S3].

Key decisions — cost-sharing levels, benefits, premiums — would be made by a nine-member appointed Federal Health Board whose rules take effect with the force of law unless Congress passes a disapproval resolution, shifting major policy choices away from Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the largest possible in health policy: universal coverage, elimination of medical bills as a cause of hardship, and long-term care protection, financed progressively. The costs are real: new premiums and payroll costs, the disruption of a system nearly 200 million people depended on, and concentration of enormous power in appointed boards. A reasonable person could support it or oppose it on the merits; the objection is not that the design is dishonest, but that the transition risk was large and the financing was left largely to unelected boards to set in detail.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got one hearing in June 1992, and the committee never reported it out before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the American Health Security Plan on April 2, 1992, joined by two cosponsors, Senators Wofford and Simon [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee held hearings on June 17, 1992, but never marked up or reported the bill [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, and the bill expired with it [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep the market the bill would have closed, and employers keep their tax-favored health plans. The roughly 37 million Americans then without coverage — the number widely reported for the era — remained uninsured; nothing in this record changed their position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and employers with health plans

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, authoring a universal public health insurance plan that would replace Medicare, Medicaid, and most private coverage.

for.name: Sens. Harris Wofford and Paul Simon

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, held one hearing on June 17, 1992, and never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have eliminated duplicative private coverage and the employer tax deduction for non-public plans, removing private insurers from their main market; opposition to single-payer proposals of this era was well documented.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the party split can only be seen in sponsorship: all three sponsors were Democrats, and the bill never left a committee controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill bars private coverage of services the public plan already covers and strips the tax deduction from employer group plans that are not the public program, moving Americans' basic coverage entirely into the public system. Insurers would be left only supplemental products, so their core business would end.

Employers would pay premiums scaled to workforce size and profitability, but would stop paying premiums to insurers and lose the administrative burden of running health plans. The employer-based system they control today would be dismantled.

Every resident would be a paying patient, ending uncompensated care, but payment would come through negotiated global operating, capital, and training budgets rather than fee-for-service billing, capping institutional revenue.

Doctors would get guaranteed payment with no patient bad debt, but must accept the negotiated fee schedule as payment in full (mandatory assignment), and reimbursement rates would be set through negotiation with state boards rather than billed individually.
The bill covers nursing home, home-based, and community long-term care publicly, with income and spousal protections, removing the main reason families buy private long-term care policies.
